questions.text: Architect C's architectural drawings and design images were copied to a project website without permission and remain online. The unauthorized use began five years before discovery. What remedy framing is most source-safe under RA 8293?

options.text: The architect must accept the use because any online infringement older than three years eliminates all remedies
The architect may seek an injunction to stop continuing infringement and may seek damages subject to RA 8293 proof and timing rules
The architect can only demand removal because monetary remedies are never available for online publication
All legal action is barred once the use has continued for five years, even if the material remains online

rationale.a: This overstates the time issue; RA 8293 has a damages limit, not a blanket rule that erases every possible remedy.
rationale.c: Section 216 includes monetary remedies; removal is not the only civil remedy.
rationale.d: This treats the four-year damages limit as a total bar to all relief, which the local source does not support.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 177 protects economic rights such as reproduction, public display, and communication to the public. Section 216 allows injunction and damages/profits remedies. Section 226 limits damages recovery after four years from the time the cause of action arose, so the source-safe answer preserves prospective relief and treats damages as timing- and proof-dependent.
rationale.takeaway: Long-running unauthorized use requires a remedies analysis: injunction may stop continuing infringement, while damages are subject to RA 8293 limits.

questions.text: Architect A created a distinctive hotel design with a unique curved facade and innovative interior spatial flow. Architect B, without authorization, created a new building with an identical curved facade and nearly identical interior spatial arrangement. Can Architect A pursue infringement remedies under RA 8293?

options.text: No, because buildings are functional structures that cannot be protected by copyright, unless they contain significant artistic elements
Yes, if Architect A can prove Architect B copied the specific creative expression, not merely the functional concept
Only if Architect A had registered the design with IPOPHL before Architect B's work began, ensuring legal protection under intellectual property laws
No, because the functional building code requirements make the design inherently non-protected, unless it can be shown to have artistic merit

rationale.a: Buildings and architectural works are expressly included in RA 8293; the functional nature of a building does not remove all protection.
rationale.c: RA 8293 Section 172.2 protects works by the sole fact of creation; registration is not stated as a condition for copyright to exist.
rationale.d: Functional or code-required similarities are not enough, but distinctive copied expression can be protected.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 protects works of architecture and plans or three-dimensional works relative to architecture, but Section 175 excludes ideas, systems, methods, concepts, principles, and mere data as such. Section 186 specifically covers erection of a building reproducing the whole or a substantial part of a protected architectural work. The claim depends on copying protected expression, not merely using the same functional concept.
rationale.takeaway: Architectural copyright analysis asks whether protected expression was copied, not whether the buildings share a generic function.

questions.text: What does RA 8293 protect in an architectural design?

options.text: Only the functional arrangement of rooms required by building codes, without regard to aesthetic elements
Only the construction method and structural system used, excluding any creative or artistic aspects
The architect's original creative expression in spatial design, aesthetic treatment, and distinctive conceptualization
The cost estimate and project schedule developed by the architect, including all financial projections

rationale.a: Code-required functional arrangements are not the protected creative expression.
rationale.b: Construction methods and structural systems as systems or methods are not protected by copyright as such.
rationale.d: Cost estimates and schedules are not the architectural expression being tested here.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 172 includes works of architecture and plans, sketches, charts, and three-dimensional works relative to architecture. Section 175 excludes ideas, procedures, systems, methods, concepts, principles, discoveries, and mere data as such. The protected subject is original expression, not generic functional requirements or construction methods.
rationale.takeaway: RA 8293 protects original architectural expression; it does not protect a bare idea, method, or code-mandated function.

questions.text: How long does copyright protection for architectural works extend under RA 8293?

options.text: For 20 years from the date the design is first created and registered with the Intellectual Property Office
For the lifetime of the architect plus 50 years after the architect's death
For 50 years from the date the building is completed and granted a certificate of occupancy
Only for 10 years unless the building remains in continuous use and the architect renews registration

rationale.c: This measures from building completion instead of the author's death.
rationale.d: This invents a short renewable term tied to continued building use.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 213.1 protects works under Sections 172 and 173 during the life of the author and for fifty years after death. For an individual architect's architectural work, the exam-safe term is lifetime plus 50 years after death, not 70 years and not a term measured from registration, completion, or occupancy.
rationale.takeaway: For individual architects, Section 213.1 uses life of the author plus 50 years.

questions.text: Under RA 8293, when does copyright protection attach to an architectural work covered by Section 172?

options.text: Only after copyright registration is completed with the relevant government office
Only after the building is completed and occupied
By the sole fact of creation, regardless of the mode or form of expression
Only after the design is published in a professional journal

rationale.a: Registration is not the condition stated in Section 172.2.
rationale.b: A work may be protected before a building is completed or occupied.
rationale.d: Publication in a professional journal is not the trigger under Section 172.2.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 172.2 states that works are protected by the sole fact of their creation, irrespective of mode or form of expression, content, quality, or purpose. Registration, completion, occupation, and publication are not stated as prerequisites for copyright protection to attach.
rationale.takeaway: The source phrase to remember is protection by the sole fact of creation.

questions.text: An architect created distinctive building designs in 1990. The architect died in 2015. Under RA 8293, when does copyright in these works expire?

options.text: In 2040 (25 years after creation), which confuses ordinary architectural works with the separate applied-art term
In 2035 (20 years after creation), which is not the RA 8293 copyright term for this work
In 2065 (50 years after the architect's death under RA 8293 Section 213.1)
Copyright in architectural works never expires under Philippine law

rationale.a: This uses the 25-year applied-art rule instead of Section 213.1 for the stated individual architect.
rationale.d: RA 8293 gives a long term, not perpetual copyright.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 213.1 protects works under Sections 172 and 173 during the life of the author and for fifty years after death. The architect died in 2015, so the 50-year post-mortem period runs to 2065. The date of creation does not control this individual-author term.
rationale.takeaway: For individual architects, add 50 years to the author's death year.

questions.text: An architect knows copyright protection exists by creation under RA 8293, but records copyright-related documents after dissemination or assignment. What is the source-safe purpose of that recording/deposit step?

options.text: It extends the copyright term beyond the statutory period
It creates an official record or notice for deposit, assignment, or exclusive license documents without making registration the source of copyright
It is the only way an architect can ever enforce a copyright claim
It gives the architect a monopoly over all similar building concepts

rationale.a: Recording or deposit does not extend the statutory term.
rationale.c: Section 172.2 contradicts the idea that registration is the source of copyright.
rationale.d: Copyright does not protect all similar concepts or functional ideas.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 172.2 protects works by the sole fact of creation. Sections 182 and 191 address filing or deposit records for assignments, exclusive licenses, and disseminated works. Those record steps support documentation and notice; they do not create copyright, extend the term, or protect generic concepts.
rationale.takeaway: Recording supports evidence and notice; creation is the source of copyright protection under Section 172.2.

questions.text: An architect's moral rights under RA 8293 include attribution and objection to prejudicial distortion. Which scenario most clearly tests a moral-rights violation?

options.text: A building owner performs routine maintenance by replacing worn exterior wall finishes with matching materials
A building owner adds interior building services without changing the public attribution or distinctive design expression
A building owner removes the architect's attribution from public use of the work and presents the design without credit
A building owner replaces windows while maintaining the original mullion pattern and design character

rationale.a: Routine like-for-like maintenance does not by itself show lack of attribution or prejudicial distortion.
rationale.b: Interior services may be a functional change; more facts are needed before treating it as a Section 193 violation.
rationale.d: Maintaining the original design character weakens, rather than proves, an integrity claim.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 193 gives the author the right to require attribution as far as practicable and to object to prejudicial distortion or mutilation. Removing the architect's attribution from public use of the work directly tests attribution. Routine maintenance or functional upgrades require separate facts before they become prejudicial distortion.
rationale.takeaway: Moral-rights questions usually turn on attribution or prejudicial distortion, not ordinary maintenance.

questions.text: How do RA 9266 Section 33 and RA 8293 work together in protecting architectural intellectual property?

options.text: They are mutually exclusive; an architect must choose only one statute in every case
RA 9266 IRR Section 33 gives the architecture-document consent rule, while RA 8293 supplies the broader copyright framework, assignment rules, moral rights, term, and remedies
RA 9266 is the exclusive source of architectural copyright and RA 8293 is irrelevant to architects
RA 8293 applies only to literary works and excludes architectural designs

rationale.a: The statutes can operate together; they are not mutually exclusive.
rationale.c: RA 8293 expressly includes architecture and plans relative to architecture.
rationale.d: RA 8293 Section 172 includes works of architecture and plans, sketches, charts, and three-dimensional works relative to architecture.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 IRR Section 33 treats signed, stamped, or sealed drawings, specifications, and other contract documents as the architect's intellectual property documents and requires written consent for duplication for repetition or other projects. RA 8293 supplies the broader copyright framework: protected architectural works and plans, ownership, assignment, moral rights, term, and remedies.
rationale.takeaway: Use RA 9266 Section 33 for professional-document consent; use RA 8293 for the copyright framework.

questions.text: An architectural firm assigned economic copyright in a commercial-complex design to the developer by written agreement. What rights may still remain with the architect-author under RA 8293?

options.text: The architect-author may still assert non-assignable moral rights such as attribution and integrity, but not the assigned economic licensing rights
The architect-author keeps all economic copyright despite the written assignment
The architect-author may enforce economic copyright against the developer whenever the developer licenses the design
The architect-author retains moral rights only if the assignment agreement expressly reserved them

rationale.c: This treats assigned economic rights as if they remained with the assignor.
rationale.d: Moral rights are statutory; they are not dependent on an express reservation in the assignment.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 180 allows economic copyright assignment in whole or in part. Sections 193 and 198 keep moral rights personal to the author and state that they are not assignable or subject to license. Section 195 allows waiver only within statutory limits. After assignment, the architect-author may still have moral-rights claims, but the assigned economic licensing rights belong to the assignee within the assignment scope.
rationale.takeaway: Assignment transfers economic rights within its scope; moral rights remain personal and non-assignable.
